steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a paper asking whether large language models can tell if a scientific abstract supports or refutes a hypothesis, with case studies from the social sciences. Motivate the task, relate it to prior NLP work, and list our contributions and main finding.

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Turning scholarly research findings into actionable, evidence-based impacts depends on iterative refinement, so that a given phenomenon is understood robustly across multiple studies, contexts, and so on. This sequential approach to scientific interrogation is also at the heart of null hypothesis significance testing. A hypothesis is an informed theory, or an educated guess, that is based on available information and prior findings. So the synthesis and understanding of the current literature is essential to study planning and to efficient research in general. But scholarly databases fail to aggregate, compare, contrast, and contextualize existing studies in a way that lets someone comprehensively review the relevant literature for a targeted research question. Part of the reason is that the sheer volume of published work is hard to navigate, and part is that the narrative format in which most empirical work is reported was not envisioned with machine readability in mind.

Work in natural language processing (NLP) and natural language understanding (NLU) has come up to address different challenges related to synthesizing scientific findings. For example, automated approaches for fact-checking have gotten a lot of attention in the context of misinformation and disinformation. The fact-checking task aims to assess how accurate a factual claim is based on a literature. But there are still no methods to determine whether a research question is addressed within a paper based on its abstract, and if it is, whether the corresponding hypothesis is supported or refuted by the work. In this work we propose this task, and we call it scientific hypothesis evidencing (SHE).

- Grassroots efforts
  - shared Google docs, contributed by authors of related work, socialized mainly via Twitter
  - synthesize work testing closely-related hypotheses / similar question, e.g. Does social media cause political polarization?
  - chapters add structure: similar outcomes or similar experimental settings
- This work
  - can state-of-the-art NLU and LLMs supplant manual expert-driven collaborative meta-analyses (or parts) for discerning hypotheses and findings from abstracts?
  - focus on social sciences: high quality datasets annotated by domain experts
  - contributions: (1) SHE task (evidence from abstract supporting / refuting a hypothesis); (2) benchmark dataset from expert-annotated collaborative literature reviews; (3) evaluate state of the art transfer learning and LLMs on SHE
- Finding
  - task challenging for current NLU; LLMs not better than traditional language models and transfer learning models
  - perspectives and suggestions for the path forward

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Turning scholarly research findings into actionable, evidence-based impacts depends on iterative refinement, so that a given phenomenon is understood robustly across multiple studies, contexts, and so on. This sequential approach to scientific interrogation is also at the heart of null hypothesis significance testing. A hypothesis is an informed theory, or an educated guess, that is based on available information and prior findings. So the synthesis and understanding of the current literature is essential to study planning and to efficient research in general. But scholarly databases fail to aggregate, compare, contrast, and contextualize existing studies in a way that lets someone comprehensively review the relevant literature for a targeted research question. Part of the reason is that the sheer volume of published work is hard to navigate, and part is that the narrative format in which most empirical work is reported was not envisioned with machine readability in mind.

Work in natural language processing (NLP) and natural language understanding (NLU) has come up to address different challenges related to synthesizing scientific findings. For example, automated approaches for fact-checking have gotten a lot of attention in the context of misinformation and disinformation. The fact-checking task aims to assess how accurate a factual claim is based on a literature. But there are still no methods to determine whether a research question is addressed within a paper based on its abstract, and if it is, whether the corresponding hypothesis is supported or refuted by the work. In this work we propose this task, and we call it scientific hypothesis evidencing (SHE).

There have also been grassroots efforts to assemble the literature in a useful way, for example shared Google docs that authors of related work contribute to and that are socialized mostly via Twitter. In these documents, the authors synthesize existing work that tests closely-related hypotheses or a similar research question, for example Does social media cause political polarization? These collaborative documents have chapters, which add more structure by highlighting studies with similar outcomes or similar experimental settings.

In this work we study whether, and to what extent, state-of-the-art NLU and large language models can supplant manual expert-driven collaborative meta-analyses, or parts of them, when it comes to discerning hypotheses and primary findings from scientific abstracts. We focus on the social sciences because high quality datasets annotated by domain experts are available. Our main contributions are:

- 1. We propose the SHE task, which is identifying evidence from the abstract of a scientific publication that supports or refutes a hypothesis;

- 2. We build and share a benchmark dataset for SHE using expert-annotated collaborative literature reviews;

- 3. We use this dataset to evaluate the performance of state of the art transfer learning and large language models (LLMs) on the SHE task.

What we find suggests that the task is challenging for current NLU, and LLMs do not seem to do better than traditional language models and transfer learning models. We give perspectives and suggestions for the path forward.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Translating scholarly research findings into actionable, evidence-based impacts relies on iterative refinement for a robust understanding of a given phenomenon across multiple studies, contexts, etc. This sequential approach to scientific interrogation is also at the heart of null hypothesis significance testing: a hypothesis is an informed theory, or an educated guess, based on available information and prior findings [1]. As such, synthesis and understanding of the current literature is essential to study planning and to efficient research more broadly. Yet scholarly databases fail to aggregate, compare, contrast, and contextualize existing studies in a way that allows a comprehensive review of the relevant literature in service to a targeted research question. In part, this is because the sheer volume of published work is difficult to navigate, and the narrative format through which most empirical work is reported was not envisioned with machine readability in mind.

Work in natural language processing (NLP) and natural language understanding (NLU) has emerged to address various challenges related to synthesizing scientific findings. Automated approaches for fact-checking [2], for example, have received significant attention in the context of misinformation and disinformation. This task aims to assess the accuracy of a factual claim based on a literature [3]. What remains a gap, however, are methods to determine whether a research question is addressed within a paper based on its abstract and, if so, whether the corresponding hypothesis is supported or refuted by the work. In this work, we propose this task as scientific hypothesis evidencing (SHE).

Notably, grassroots efforts to assemble the literature usefully have popped up, e.g., shared Google docs contributed to by authors of related work and socialized primarily via Twitter [4]. In these documents, authors synthesize existing work that tests closely-related hypotheses or a similar research question, e.g., Does social media cause political polarization? Chapters within these collaborative documents add further structure, highlighting studies with similar outcomes or similar experimental settings.

In this work, we study whether and to what extent state-of-the-art NLU and large language models can supplant manual expert-driven collaborative meta-analyses, or parts thereof, in discerning hypotheses and primary findings from scientific abstracts. We focus on the social sciences because of the availability of high quality datasets annotated by domain experts. Our primary contributions are as follows:

- 1. We propose the SHE task–the identification of evidence from the abstract of a scientific publication in support or refute of a hypothesis;

- 2. We build and share a benchmark dataset for SHE using expert-annotated collaborative literature reviews;

- 3. Using this dataset, we evaluate the performance of state of the art transfer learning and large language models (LLMs) on the SHE task.

Our findings suggest that this task is challenging for current NLU and that LLMs do not seem to perform better than traditional language models and transfer learning models. We offer perspectives and suggestions for the path forward.

References:
[1] Wald (1992) Abraham Wald. 1992. Sequential tests of statistical hypotheses. In Breakthroughs in statistics: Foundations and basic theory , pages 256–298. Springer.
[2] Guo et al. (2022) Zhijiang Guo, Michael Schlichtkrull, and Andreas Vlachos. 2022. A survey on automated fact-checking. Transactions of the Association for Computational Linguistics , 10:178–206.
[3] Vladika and Matthes (2023) Juraj Vladika and Florian Matthes. 2023. Scientific fact-checking: A survey of resources and approaches. arXiv preprint arXiv:2305.16859 .
[4] Haidt and Bail (2022) Jonathan Haidt and Christopher Bail. 2022. Social media and political dysfunction: A collaborative review. Unpublished manuscript, New York University .
